questions.prompt: Risk-based testing allocates effort according to:

options.text: Impact if it breaks × likelihood of failure (complexity/churn)
Whichever code is easiest to test
The number of lines of code only

questions.explanation: Concentrate testing where a failure is costly and where mistakes are likely; go light where risk is trivial.

questions.prompt: What does 'catch the bug at the lowest useful level' recommend?

options.text: Prefer the cheapest test (often a unit test) that still gives real confidence

questions.explanation: Pushing a check to the lowest level that catches the bug keeps it fast and precise, reserving E2E for critical journeys.

questions.prompt: Order the response to a newly reported bug.

items.text: Write a failing test that reproduces the bug
Fix the code until the test passes
Keep the test as a regression guard

questions.explanation: Reproduce first, then fix, and the test remains to prevent the bug from returning silently.

questions.prompt: When is deliberately NOT writing a test reasonable? Select all that apply.

options.text: Trivial code with no logic (a plain getter)
Third-party library internals you don't own

questions.explanation: Skip trivial code, throwaway spikes, and others' internals; the high-impact payment/auth path is exactly where you should test hard.

questions.prompt: A test added to lock in a fix so a bug can't return is called a ____ test.
questions.explanation: Turning each bug into a regression test builds a suite that remembers every past mistake.

questions.prompt: Match each quality of a maintainable suite to why it matters.
questions.explanation: Speed, determinism, readability, and behavior-focus are what make a suite an asset rather than a tax.
